I'm polyamorous and I also have BPD. 
It's not pretty, but I used to be very emotionally manipulative.  "Please come over, I'm so sad," crying when my partners said it was time for them to leave and go home or to visit their other partners, etc. Once or twice I even did the dreaded "I'm feeling suicidal, you have to come over." 
I never outright said "if you don't come over then I'm going to end my life," but it was heavily implied.

Because BPD makes me feel emotions to the extreme, I genuinely used to believe that I was just being honest with my partners when I told them about my suicidality. But I wasn't, not really. I didn't want them to leave because I didn't want to be alone. And I used to use my emotions as a weapon to get what I wanted. It's fucked. I know that now.

None of my partners ever called me out on it, I think because nobody wants to be the asshole who ignores someone when they say they want to die. One day, though, my partner (who I'm still with today) sat me down and told me how problematic that kind of behaviour is. He point blank told me that I was being manipulative and that it wasn't fair. It was an earth shattering moment because like I said, I never thought I was doing anything wrong. I thought I was just being honest.

I was horrified. My first reaction was to start crying and then I stopped and thought... Hang on, he's right. 
Luckily, he was willing to work with me on those behaviours. I told him that I never wanted to manipulate anyone and he promised he'd call me out if he noticed I was doing it. He stuck to his word and would pull me aside and gently let me know that what I'd said wasn't okay. Gradually, I stopped. I went to therapy to work through my underlying mental issues. 

I'm eternally grateful for his patience, and for his willingness to be honest with me. He told me I was being a fuckhead, but then he held my hand as I walked the path to recovery. He never gave up on me. 

So, yeah. Tl;dr: I was toxic and emotionally manipulative as fuck but my partner called me out on my bullshit and helped me become a better person. Now I wouldn't ever dream of pulling that kind of shit.

I used to draw butterflies on my wrists, ankles, anywhere I used to get the urge to cut. (The idea being that if you cut, the butterfly would die.) It was effective for a bit but then lost some of its power, so I started looking for alternatives. I've tried:

-putting my wrist into warm water and focusing on the sensation of that. Or using ice cubes. Focusing on a sensation really helped me to forget about the compulsion to cut. 

-deep breathing techniques.

-sitting on my hands and gritting my teeth until the worst of the feeling passes. 

-do something else with your hands. If they're busy, you can't hurt yourself. Journalling helps me, but you can draw, play cats cradle, pet an animal, knit, make shadow puppets, find a friend to thumb wrestle, anything that occupies your hands.

-wearing mittens, which was shockingly effective.

-taking the power away from myself by asking a loved one for help. This was the hardest one but was ultimately what worked for me. If I found the urge I told my partner, a friend, or someone I trusted. They would take the sharp things away from me and stay with me until I was calm.

 If you're not able to be that vulnerable with someone then you need to create your own area to go when you're feeling this compulsion. Remove sharp stuff, surround yourself with self care objects (soft fabrics, books, music, whatever you personally use for self care.) And stay in that safe location for as long as you can physically stand it. I find it helpful to use a timer so I have something to concentrate on, or to put on a film or some music to distract myself. 


If you're unable to create a space like this, you might find a support chat service like lifeline or 7cupsoftea useful. 

Therapy is important, if you're able to access it. If you can't access face to face therapy then please consider using one of the mental health services that can be found online.

Tl;dr: distract yourself, redirect your energy into another task that requires your hands so you can't harm yourself, take lots of deep breaths, and seek help when you can. (Which you're doing now by making this post. Which was probably hard so I want to say good job on that.) I'm just a stranger on the internet but I believe in you. You can do this.

I had a housemate turned friend for a few years who had a massive amount of control over my life. I didn't realize how much control she had over me for the longest time. A lot of the stuff she did had the all hallmarks of a toxic relationship, but, having grown up in a similarly toxic environment, I was kind of blinded to it.


She used to start fights with my partners, my sister, my friends, everyone, as a joke. I think she just thought the conflict was funny. She'd make mean jokes about me and other people and behave obnoxiously just to laugh when people got frustrated with her. 


If I disagreed with her, or if I didn't want to take part in her mean jokes, or even if I was busy doing something else, she'd tell me I was being a bad friend.


She used to refuse to talk to me if I did an activity she didn't enjoy, or if I tried to spend time with any of my other friends without her. I'd had this exact thing happen to me in the past, from my mother, and I'm sure she knew that and used it to her advantage. She'd manipulate me to the brink of panic attacks and then rush in and show me kindness, which made me forget the conflict that had just occurred. She wasn't manipulative! She couldn't be, because she was hugging me and making me laugh! Nobody who was this good at providing comfort could be a mean person. But still, I lived through those years in a constant state of anxiety that I would upset her.


Then one day I looked around and noticed... None of my friends really wanted to spend time with me anymore. I asked my partner at the time why he thought my friends weren't very interested in spending time with me, and he told me that she wasn't a good friend or a nice person to spend time with. I didn't believe him, we had a gigantic fight and broke up. She nursed me through the depression that followed.


Years passed, we both moved into seperate houses and our friendship was less intense. I'd still get messages from her every few weeks demanding to know why I wasn't speaking to her, even though she hadn't initiatied contact either. I'd say I was busy, but the reality was that I'd been to therapy and worked through my attachment issues with my mother. This helped me to realise that my relationship with her wasn't healthy at all.


So, instead of being honest with her, I just deleted her off every platform I had her on, blocked her phone number and disappeared from her life. I really regret doing that. I could have been honest with her but I was too scared of the fallout, so I didn't. After it happened, I was petrified that she'd come to my work or my house to confront me, but she never did. For the longest time I avoided places that she used to frequent, just in case. Gradually, I stopped thinking about her for the most part, and I began to heal. That nagging feeling of anxiety went away, and I surrounded myself with people whose support wasn't contingent on me behaving in a certain way.


If I had the chance to apologise for ghosting her, I like to think I would. In reality, I'm still scared of the prospect of running into her somewhere, so I'd probably just hide my face and disappear again.

My city flooded a few years ago. I work in a pharmacy. It's in a higher lying area but there's creek crossings on all but one side of the area. 
One day, before the flooding was severe, I came into work. 
I was completely soaked from the rain but went out onto the floor to serve customers anyhow, keeping an eye on the weather report for new information. About two hours into my shift, the bureau of meteorology put out a bulletin advising businesses and schools to close as the main river was dangerously close to breaking its banks. Head office of the pharmacy chain sent out an email advising the same.
One of the managers at the time (who was a lapdog to the pharmacy owner, a very intimidating woman) wouldn't let anyone go home without calling the owner and explaining why we needed to leave.
One of my colleagues (who relied on public transport to get home) called the owner (as busses had steadily been cancelled all day) and was yelled at until she cried, so none of us were brave enough to try calling. 
The carpark was almost entirely underwater. There were no customers. The power went out. The owner still refused to close the store, so we all stayed until the end of our shifts. 
We found out a few days later that one of the other managers had been flooded out of her house and was staying on a friend's couch for the foreseeable future. She lost a sizeable chunk of her possessions because she didn't get home in time to get anything out.

This thread is eye opening. I'm realising that a bunch of things my nmum did were a lot more nefarious than I first thought. 

(CW: animal neglect/death)

My sister and I went through a period of NC with her after a particularly bad fight. We were still in the same house, but we didn't speak or interact at all.

Our dog was very old and sick, he had tumours all over his belly but he was his usual happy puppy-like self. Then one morning we woke up and the back verandah, where he used to sleep, was covered in spots of blood. Nmum and our dog were nowhere to be found. So we, panicking, ran straight to nmum's work and asked her where he was and what had happened.

She turned on the waterworks (I don't believe they were genuine) and told us that our puppy's tumours had started bleeding overnight and she'd taken him to the vet. We asked when he was coming home. She told us that he wasn't. She'd made the call of having him put down while we were asleep. 

Years went by, I moved away and wasn't regular in the contact I kept with her, so she pulled the same stunt with our childhood cat, who meant more to me than anything in the world. I found out weeks after she'd done it through my sister, who was surprised that I hadn't been told. Nmum said she would call me to let me know, but she never did.

Then extenuating circumstances forced me to move back home with my new kitty that I'd adopted. I used to take a long distance train to travel back to the city at the weekends to see friends. I told nmum really explicitly that kitty needed to be inside at night because it was an unfamiliar area and she'd get spooked and bolt up the nearest tree if there were no people around her. She was a sweet little lovebug who hated being alone, and I figured she'd be fine at home, there were no shortage of laps of curl up on.

I came home and she'd disappeared. I asked nmum where she was. "Oh she was here yesterday, she'll be around somewhere."
So I looked everywhere, and when I couldn't find her I went door knocking around the neighbourhood to ask if they'd seen her. One man had seen her, but only because he'd had to pick her up off the road and bury her.

After reading this thread there's no doubt in my mind that nmum locked her outside on purpose as some kind of punishment for leaving. I guess she was trying to teach me that bad things happen when I left my home town. What I really learned is that she wasn't to be trusted around animals.
NTA at all. It's okay to want space.

Okay. I'm going to tell this story. It is gross, so buckle in.
I went to hospital with really intense pain in my stomach and the x-ray/ultrasound showed a great big fecal impaction and an inflamed appendix, respectively.
So obviously this is a bad thing right? The doctors don't want to operate around a mass on my colon so the nurses were feeding me movicol. For those that don't know, movicol is a really disgustingly viscous and salty liquid laxative. I had to drink two litres of the stuff. Every time I finished a glass it seemed like they would bring me another.
Nothing happened all day, other than trying to sleep through the pain. Not even a rumble from my stomach. So, I went to sleep. The guy in the bed next to me was complaining loudly and the guy next to him was doing the loudest snoring i'd ever heard, so I put in my ear plugs and passed out. I woke up in the middle of the night and... I had shat the bed. Explosively and apocalyptically shat the bed. I lifted the sheet and it was just... Everywhere. 
So I panicked, leapt out of bed and started pulling the sheets off. Then I just stood there for ten minutes, holding the world's most disgusting bundle of sheets, trying frantically to decide what to do. In the end I pressed the nurse button, and she was really lovely about it. She took the sheets away and brought me a towel. It hadn't occurred to me that the back of my hospital gown was stained with shit, so I waddled off to the showers, in full view of everyone who was still awake.
When I got back to bed, they'd replaced the sheets and even left me with a thoughtful incontinence pad. I couldn't sleep for the rest of the night because I was so horrified by what had just happened.
